case_study_insert.main_stem: Quentin Metal Fasteners (QMF) is a private limited company in the industrial fasteners sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2003 by Sofia Quentin, it produces high-strength threaded bolts and nuts for construction equipment and railway suppliers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, exporting to nearby markets. QMF plans to invest $640,000 in an automated bolt-threading line, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit, with an overdraft facility for working capital. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $10 a unit and a selling price of $19, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. QMF faces two problems: labour turnover of 14% and a defect rate of 3.6% on threaded bolts.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q3 2025: The line threaded 15,000 high-strength bolts last quarter at a defect rate of 3.6%, down from 5.2% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 34 to 19 a month and average delivery time is 4.1 days. A survey of 350 industrial distributors found 62% value certified thread tolerance and 55% prefer a local supplier. A new quality control inspection regime is being introduced on the line; labour turnover reached 14%, and an external quality-audit training course costs $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Quentin Metal Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 an hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Steel wire rod input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, producer price inflation is 5.5%, and demand from industrial distributors grew 3.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: QMF plans to fund its $640,000 bolt-threading line with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for QMF of using the bank loan instead of its overdraft facility.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bank loan gives QMF a fixed repayment schedule spread over the life of the $640,000 threading line, so the cost of the asset is matched by steady outflows that can be planned alongside fixed costs of $270,000 a year. An overdraft is repayable on demand and is meant for short-term working capital; using it for a long-lived asset would leave Sofia Quentin unsure when the money might be called back, just as the line needs to produce 60,000 units.

Point 2: Bank loan interest is normally lower than overdraft interest, so choosing the $400,000 loan keeps finance charges down and protects the $9 contribution on each bolt. That matters when labour turnover is 14% and the defect rate is 3.6%, both of which already cost money. The $240,000 of retained profit also lowers the amount borrowed, so the firm keeps headroom on its overdraft for the 4.1-day delivery gap instead of exhausting it on capital equipment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QMF's investment, costs and working-capital position.

questions.question_text: QMF is expanding sales of certified bolts. Consider a direct sales force, regional industrial distributors, or an online industrial marketplace. Which should QMF choose to reach industrial distributors? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Direct sales force: Employing sales engineers would let QMF explain certified thread tolerance face to face and build long-term relationships with construction and railway buyers. This suits a technical product and the 62% of surveyed distributors who value certification. However, salaries, travel and commissions are a heavy fixed cost for a 48-employee firm funding a $640,000 line with a $400,000 loan, and covering the whole region would take years.

Regional industrial distributors: Distributors already hold stock and contacts, so QMF can reach buyers quickly without employing a large sales team, and the 55% who prefer a local supplier are reached through local warehousing. The drawback is that distributors take a margin and control the customer relationship, which weakens QMF's ability to communicate the quality control improvements that cut defects from 5.2% to 3.6%.

Online industrial marketplace: A marketplace listing gives national visibility at low fixed cost, displays certification to the 62% who value it, and generates measurable orders from the 350 distributors surveyed. It fits standard high-strength bolts made at 15,000 a quarter and can be scaled as the threading line beds in. The weakness is price comparison with rivals and reduced personal service for railway contracts.

Recommendation: QMF should choose regional industrial distributors as the main channel, supported by a small marketplace listing. Distributors give immediate local reach and hold stock, which matches the 55% preference for local suppliers and the 4.1-day delivery expectation, while the marketplace adds low-cost visibility. A direct sales force is rejected because its fixed salary cost cannot be justified on a $400,000-loan-funded expansion, and a marketplace alone cannot service the relationship-based railway contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three distribution channels with minimal application to QMF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two channels in the context of QMF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three channels in the context of QMF with a justified recommendation explaining why a direct sales force and a pure marketplace are rejected.

questions.question_text: QMF has a defect rate of 3.6% and labour turnover of 14%. Explain two benefits for QMF of using inspection-based quality control on its threading line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Inspection catches faulty threads before bolts leave the line, so QMF can protect the improvement from 5.2% to 3.6% defects and avoid sending bad batches to the 350 industrial distributors surveyed. With inspection being introduced on the line, operators who understand why bolts are rejected are likelier to correct faults at source, reducing the $750 training cost needed later. Fewer rejects mean more of the 15,000 bolts a quarter are saleable at $19, defending the $9 contribution per unit and reducing the waste that hurts a 48-employee firm.

Point 2: A visible inspection regime gives clear quality targets to an autocratic, hierarchical workforce, which can steadier output while labour turnover is 14%. Inspectors can feed defects back to operators quickly and link results to the $750 external quality-audit course, so new staff reach the required tolerance faster and the $640,000 threading line does not lose orders because of inconsistent certified quality. Fewer leavers also mean less disruption to the 4.1-day delivery promise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to QMF's defect rate, turnover and certification.

questions.question_text: QMF needs a manager to run quality on the new threading line. Consider promoting an existing worker or recruiting a qualified specialist from outside. Which should QMF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Promoting an existing worker: An internal candidate already knows QMF's machines, the 3.6% defect problem and the expectations of the 350 distributors, so induction is short and morale may rise because staff see a career path — useful when turnover is 14%. Promotion is also cheap, avoiding recruitment fees. The risk is that the worker lacks formal audit skills, and the $750 quality-audit course may not be enough to manage certification claims or to challenge long-standing habits under autocratic leadership.

Recruiting a qualified specialist from outside: An external quality manager brings current audit methods and an unbiased eye, which suits the 62% of distributors who value certified thread tolerance and supports the $640,000 investment. Drawbacks are higher salary, a longer settling-in period, and possible resentment among the 48 staff, especially when a promotion route would have helped retention.

Decision: QMF should promote an existing worker and send that person on the $750 external quality-audit course, with a short mentoring spell from a consultant. This keeps cost low, rewards loyalty at a time when turnover is 14%, and preserves knowledge of the line that cut defects from 5.2% to 3.6%. External recruitment is rejected because the added salary and disruption are hard to justify on a $400,000-loan-funded expansion when training can close the specific skills gap; the specialist can be hired later if certification demands grow. That keeps the $750 course budget focused on the 14% turnover problem and avoids a second salary while the $640,000 line is still settling in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment choices with limited application to QMF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both choices in the context of QMF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both choices in the context of QMF with a justified decision covering cost, skills and staff retention.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QMF's management can use its cost and break-even data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($19 − $10) = $270,000 ÷ $9 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $19 − $10 = $9. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways QMF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even of 30,000 units with output of 60,000 units gives a margin of safety of 30,000 units, showing how far sales can fall before losses begin while the $640,000 line is commissioned.
2. Contribution of $9 a bolt lets managers model a distributor discount: a $0.50 reduction would leave $8.50, so they can calculate the extra volume needed to cover $270,000 fixed costs before agreeing terms with the 350 surveyed distributors.
3. The $400,000 bank loan can be judged against the 30,000-unit break-even: every bolt above that point adds $9, so managers can check that the line generates enough contribution to service borrowing.
4. Unit cost ($270,000 ÷ 60,000 units + $10 = $13.50 a bolt) gives a benchmark for the 15,000 bolts made last quarter, helping measure the cost of the 3.6% defect rate and decide whether to challenge the $10 variable cost amid 9.4% steel input inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 30,000 units against 60,000 output; distributor discount modelling on the $9 contribution; loan servicing on the $400,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.50 to attack the 3.6% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QMF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has QMF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $200,000; 2025 current assets = $80,000 + $110,000 + $50,000 = $240,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $160,000 in both years gives 1.25 and 1.50. Excluding inventories: ($200,000 − $75,000) ÷ $160,000 = $125,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.78 in 2024, and ($240,000 − $80,000) ÷ $160,000 = $160,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.00 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The current ratio rose from 1.25 to 1.50 because current assets grew by $40,000 while current liabilities stayed at $160,000. The stricter measure also rose, from 0.78 to 1.00, so in 2025 QMF can cover all short-term obligations without relying on bolt inventories — helpful while it repays a $400,000 loan and installs a $640,000 threading line. Cash also rose from $30,000 to $50,000, strengthening the immediate buffer for the overdraft. There is a caveat: trade receivables rose from $95,000 to $110,000, so cash is tied up with distributors, and the overdraft facility could be drawn if those distributors pay late. Inventories also edged up to $80,000, so slow-moving stock should be monitored.

Conclusion: QMF's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the rise does not depend on stock, which is the more demanding test. The residual risk is slower collections from distributors, so credit control should be tightened before the next expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QMF of switching to recycled steel and eco-packaging for its bolts.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled steel and eco-packaging would appeal to the 62% of surveyed industrial distributors who value certified quality and the 55% who prefer responsible local suppliers, helping QMF win orders against the 9.4% rise in steel input costs. It strengthens the certified fastener brand and supports the 15,000 bolts a quarter produced on the new $640,000 line without cutting the $19 selling price.

Disadvantage: Recycled steel may vary in quality and raise the 3.6% defect rate if inclusions cause thread failures, while eco-packaging usually costs more than standard cartons, pushing up the $10 variable cost per unit. For a 48-employee firm already carrying a $400,000 loan, any extra unit cost directly reduces the $9 contribution, and buyers may not pay a premium even though 55% say they prefer local suppliers. The insert gives no evidence that a premium will actually be paid, and the 4.1-day delivery promise could suffer if alternative materials arrive late.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to QMF's survey, costs and defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in steel input costs will affect QMF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 5.00% − 4.25% = 0.75 percentage points. If the $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest = 0.75% × $400,000 = 0.0075 × $400,000 = $3,000 a year. That is modest beside fixed costs of $270,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no direct extra charge. Higher rates could make the overdraft more expensive, but a shown figure for that is not possible because the insert gives no overdraft balance or rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, $12.90 to $13.70 an hour): QMF employs a workforce of 48 and produces 60,000 units, so labour productivity = 60,000 ÷ 48 = 1,250 units per worker. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an honest annual wage cost cannot be invented. The wage rise is compulsory and will lift unit labour cost unless the 3.6% defect rate is reduced and output per worker holds at 1,250; otherwise the $9 contribution per bolt is squeezed.

Steel input-cost inflation (9.4%): The insert does not split the $10 variable cost, so only a clearly labelled upper bound can be calculated: if the entire $10 rose by 9.4%, the increase = 9.4% × $10 = 0.094 × $10 = $0.94 a bolt; at 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $0.94 = $56,400 a year. Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution on every bolt, and the $19 price may be hard to raise when 55% of distributors prefer local suppliers.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It is the only change with a computable annual exposure on every unit of $56,400 at the upper bound, directly eroding the $9 contribution that supports the $640,000 investment. The interest rise adds at most $3,000, and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity gains. Management should therefore renegotiate steel supply and seek a certified-quality premium before considering price rises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to QMF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on QMF's costs, revenue or financing with figures derived from the insert.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with shown derivations and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
